performers: Berlin Philharmonic Orchestra; Wilhelm Furtwängler, conductor
question: How differently can two performances distribute nearly ten minutes of slow music?
intro: Furtwängler and the Berlin Philharmonic recorded the Sixth Symphony in Berlin in 1938; this finale survives through a Victor 78-rpm issue. Commons supplies a recording-specific European public-domain statement, but its linked Internet Archive item is now unavailable and cannot independently establish the earlier transfer’s terms.

sections.label: Opening span
sections.mNote: measured listening spans, not a score-aligned formal map

cues.title: Time within the slow phrase
cues.text: Follow the distance between one phrase’s crest and the next beginning. Nearly equal total durations can conceal different amounts of time spent in a rise, a held note or a withdrawal.
cues.evidence: The new analysis measures 609.3 seconds against 619.0 for the Musopen file. This general comparison does not infer local tempo from total length or from the unreliable onset-tempo estimate.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Quiet makes room for renewal
cues.text: The early passage withdraws markedly before the sound returns with force. Listen through the intervening space, not only to the renewed attack; its duration helps shape the phrase.
cues.evidence: Relative level falls through 1:05–1:15 and rises sharply around 1:20. The report supports a broad contrast but not a named instrument entrance at an exact second.

cues.title: Berlin, not a documented concert
cues.text: Commons dates the recording to October–November 1938 in Berlin’s Beethovensaal. It identifies the Berlin Philharmonic and Furtwängler, but does not describe this as a live concert recording; the venue alone cannot establish an audience.
cues.evidence: The file’s Summary and carrier note give session range, place and performers, without an audience or concert claim. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Tchaikovsky_-_Path%C3%A9tique_-_Wilhelm_Furtw%C3%A4ngler_-_IV._Finale_-_Adagio_lamentoso.ogg

cues.title: A rise over several phrases
cues.text: In this broad build, distinguish continued growth from the smaller retreats inside it. The longer trajectory can remain audible even when the sound briefly falls back.
cues.evidence: The report shows increased relative level around 3:30–3:45, a partial retreat around 3:55 and renewed strength at 4:05–4:25. No continuous crescendo or precise harmonic arrival is claimed.

cues.title: A slow ending was planned
cues.text: In February 1893, Tchaikovsky told his nephew Vladimir Davydov that the finale would be a long Adagio rather than a noisy Allegro. The same letter keeps the symphony’s programme private: the music is not a documented prediction of his death.
cues.evidence: Tchaikovsky Research quotes Letter 4865, dated 11/23 February 1893, with the planned slow finale and the programme left as an enigma. https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/pages/Symphony_No._6

cues.title: The stronger sound persists
cues.text: Compare this sustained stretch of force with the earlier shorter peaks. The length of time spent near a crest can matter as much as its height; the trace describes only relative level within this transfer.
cues.evidence: The loudest five-second windows are concentrated between 6:35 and 6:55. These measurements locate the sustained region without comparing absolute loudness with the Musopen recording.

cues.title: An unavailable upstream transfer
cues.text: The Commons file links to an Internet Archive item that is now unavailable. Its explicit European recording-rights statement remains visible, but the earlier transfer’s licence and processing history cannot be independently reconstructed from that missing page.
cues.evidence: The linked archive metadata returns is_dark:true, its details page returned 404 and its metadata XML 403 on 17 October 2026. The dossier reports this limit; it does not certify the absence of earlier non-commercial restrictions. https://archive.org/metadata/TCHAIKOVSKYSymphonyNo.6Pathetique-NEWTRANSFER

cues.title: Follow the prolonged decline
cues.text: Stay with the remaining line as the sound recedes. The end is not a single cut-off: the later passage spends time withdrawing, with smaller renewals inside the overall decline.
cues.evidence: The analysis shows generally falling relative level from 9:00 through 9:55, with a local rise around 9:30; by 10:00–10:05 only very low-level signal remains. The note does not locate an exact final note.

composer.epithet: He used the timing of dance and theatre to make a symphony’s return, interruption or collapse physically audible.
facts: Imperial School of Jurisprudence; Saint Petersburg Conservatory, 1862–65, with Anton Rubinstein and Nikolai Zaremba
Nadezhda von Meck supplied an allowance from 1877 to 1890; their correspondence became a major record of his working life
Six numbered symphonies and Manfred; three ballets; operas, concertos, chamber music, piano music and songs
composer.background:
Tchaikovsky was born at Votkinsk, where his father managed an ironworks. Music belonged to the household before it became a profession: his governess Fanny Dürbach remembered the child’s intense responses to it, and he began piano lessons early. His formal training nevertheless pointed towards government service. In 1850 he entered the preparatory class of the Imperial School of Jurisprudence in Saint Petersburg, separated from his family. His mother died of cholera in 1854. After graduating in 1859 he worked in the Ministry of Justice, while concerts, opera and lessons gradually occupied more of his time.

When Anton Rubinstein’s Saint Petersburg Conservatory opened in 1862, Tchaikovsky joined its first generation of students. He studied composition with Rubinstein and theoretical subjects with Nikolai Zaremba, leaving government employment in 1863. The training mattered practically: he could organise large forms, prepare orchestral scores and teach harmony. In 1866 Nikolai Rubinstein recruited him for the new Moscow Conservatory. Tchaikovsky taught there until 1878, wrote criticism and translated pedagogical material. His early reputation grew through this sustained professional work.
